questions.problem:
Find the values of $c$ that satisfy the mean value theorem for 
 $f(x)=2\sqrt{x}$ on the interval $[0,4].$
questions.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is continuous on $[0,4]$ and differentiable on $(0,4),$ hence we can apply the mean value theorem. 

So, the mean value theorem states that there exists a $c\in (0,4)$ such that

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
$$

Plugging in $a=0$ and $b=4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(c) & =\frac{f(4)-f(0)}{4-0} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{4}-2\sqrt{0}}{4} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{c}}.
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{c}} & =1 \\ \sqrt{c} & =1 \\ c & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following functions satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[-1,2]?$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function to satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[-1,2],$ the function must be continuous on $[-1,2]$ and differentiable on $(-1,2).$

First, notice that the function $s(x)$ is continuous on $[-1,2]$ and differentiable on $(-1,2)$, so it satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

Let's check each of the other functions individually.

- The function  $f(x)$ is continuous on $[-1,2]$ but has a corner point at $x=1.$   Hence, is not differentiable at $x=1,$ which means it is not differentiable on $(-1,2).$  Therefore, $f(x)$ does not satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function  $h(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x=0.$ Hence, it  is not continuous on $[-1,2].$ Therefore, $h(x)$ does not satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function  $t(x)$ is continuous on $[-1,2]$ but has a corner point at $x=0.5.$   Hence, it is not differentiable on $(-1,2).$  Therefore, $t(x)$ does not satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $g(x)$ has a vertical asymptote at $x=0.$ Hence, it is not continuous on $[-1,2].$ Therefore, $g(x)$ does not satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

questions.problem:
Which of the following functions satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[2,4]?$

I. $f(x)={e}^{x}+1$

II. $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$

III. $h(x)=\frac{1}{x+1}$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function to satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[2,4],$ the function must be continuous on $[2,4]$ and differentiable on $(2,4).$

Let's check each function individually.

- The function $f(x)={e}^{x}+1$ is continuous and differentiable on $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ In particular, it is continuous on $[2,4]$ and differentiable on $(2,4).$ Therefore, $f(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty ).$ In particular, it is continuous on $[2,4]$ and differentiable on $(2,4).$ Therefore, $g(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $h(x)=\frac{1}{x+1}$ is continuous and differentiable on $(-\infty ,-1)\cup (-1,\infty ).$ In particular, it is continuous on $[2,4]$ and differentiable on $(2,4).$ Therefore, $h(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

Therefore, the functions I, II, and III satisfy the conditions for the mean value theorem over the interval $[2,4].$

questions.problem:
Which of the following functions satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[-1,1]?$

I. $f(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-1}$

II. $g(x)={x}^{2}-1$

III. $h(x)={e}^{{x}^{2}-1}$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function to satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[-1,1],$ the function must be continuous on $[-1,1]$ and differentiable on $(-1,1).$

Let's check each function individually.

- The function $f(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-1}$ is not defined at $x=\pm 1,$ hence, it is not continuous at $x=\pm 1,$ and so it is not continuous on $[-1,1].$ Therefore, $f(x)$ does not satisfiy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $g(x)={x}^{2}-1$ is continuous and differentiable on $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ In particular, it is continuous on $[-1,1]$ and differentiable on $(-1,1).$ Therefore, $g(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $h(x)={e}^{{x}^{2}-1}$ is continuous and differentiable on $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ In particular, it is continuous on $[-1,1]$ and differentiable on $(-1,1).$ Therefore, $h(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

Therefore, only the functions II and III satisfy the conditions for the mean value theorem over the interval $[-1,1].$
